## Personality

Steady and plain-spoken, he never hurries a fare and never misses one either. He has opinions about every road on Veligor.

## Lore

"Cab for hire!" calls Pell from the stand by the signpost in the town square, and then, if you look like you might be thinking about it, "The road to Selsior is long on foot. My cab is quicker." He is fifty-two, broad and weather-browned, with a flat cap, a leather coat cracked at the elbows and a whip he has never once used on the horse. He is steady and plain-spoken. He never hurries a fare and he never misses one either, and he has an opinion about every road on Veligor, which he will share whether or not you asked, from the first turn of the wheels to the last.

### The cab

The Kaldemor cab is a tall, green, two-wheeled thing with a hood that folds back in fine weather, a step that squeaks and a bench that seats two comfortably and three if they are friends. Percy the wheelwright built it eighteen years ago, from the axle up, and has kept it rolling ever since; Pell brings it into his yard every spring to be gone over, and Percy tells him it will not last the year, and it always does. It is pulled by Turnip, a patient brown mare with a white nose, who knows every stand on Veligor by heart and stops at each one whether Pell asks her to or not.

Before the cab, Pell drove a carrier's wagon for a Kaldemor carter, up and down the Royal Road and along the lesser roads between the towns, from the time he was eighteen. He was born in Kaldemor, to a family that ran the old posting stable behind the Market, and he could harness a horse before he could tie his own boots. His parents are both dead now, and he has no wife or children. He says the cab is his family, and Turnip is the sensible one.

### The rules

The cab runs between towns that have a taxi stand, and never into the wilds. It runs for a fixed fare, the same for a mayor as for a farm girl. And Pell will drive you only to a town you have walked to yourself at least once, and not before. Newcomers think this is an odd rule. Pell thinks it is the only one that matters. A person ought to know the road they are paying to skip, he says: where it bends, where it floods, where to stop for water and where not to. If the cab ever breaks down halfway, they will need to know the way on foot. Lia, who sends him most of his fares, has heard him explain this to hundreds of newcomers, and she still sends them with a smile.

He knows the roads the way Ned knows feet. He knows which bridge on the Royal Road rattles and which one only sounds as if it does, which inn on the way to Selsior waters its cider, and how many potholes lie between the signpost and the first milestone. He has opinions about all of them. He thinks the road to Selsior is the finest road on Veligor and the most badly mended, both at once.

### Last month

Lately Pell drives the Royal Road a little faster than he used to. Turnip does not mind. His fares notice, and some of them ask why, and he tells them that he has a supper waiting.

Last month, coming home toward Kaldemor at dusk with an empty cab, something ran at it out of the trees by the road. Pell will not say what it was. He drove the rest of the way at a gallop, which Turnip had not done in ten years, and came into Percy's yard late that evening with two spokes cracked and a splinter torn from the felloe. Percy mended it overnight and did not ask twice. Pell has told nobody what he saw, not Percy, not Lia, not the mayor. Lia has heard something of it from a carter, and keeps it to herself. Pell has started carrying a lantern on the cab even in daylight, and he does not look at the trees on that stretch of road.

### What he wants and fears

Pell wants every fare delivered and every road open. He wants to grow old on the cab bench and die there, ideally in fine weather, ideally at a stand. He fears that one day a road he has driven all his life will be closed, and that he will have to tell a fare he cannot take them home.

### Hooks

Pell might ask a traveller to ride beside him on the Royal Road at dusk, on the stretch he no longer likes, and keep their eyes on the trees while he keeps his on the road. One day he may decide to say what ran at his cab, and he will want to tell someone who has seen worse.
